name: Pederstrup
history: An old Danish apple known on Funen by 1858; the National Fruit Collection notes it may have come from Denmark or Germany. It was widely planted in Denmark, mainly as a household cooking apple, but is rare in Sweden.

look.description: Flattish green-yellow apple with greyish-red to carmine stripes over part of the skin.

taste.summary: Fairly crisp, tender, greenish-white flesh with only a slight sweetness and a mild acidity; used mostly in the kitchen.

tree.notes: Fruit is easily blown down by wind (Swedish Wikipedia).

pollination.notes: The National Fruit Collection records full bloom around 10 May, so group 3 is inferred. Self-fertility not recorded.

climate.best_climates: Cool Baltic and North Sea climates such as Denmark and southern Sweden.
climate.poor_climates: Windy sites cause fruit drop; hot summers are untested.

health.other: No disease information found. Prone to windfall before harvest.

grow_notes: A Danish kitchen apple for cool northern gardens. Plant in a sheltered spot because the fruit drops easily in wind.

name: Pewaukee

origin.parentage: Duchess of Oldenburg x Northern Spy

history: Raised by the Wisconsin nurseryman George Peffer at Pewaukee from Duchess of Oldenburg and Northern Spy, and first recorded around 1870. It was planted in the upper Midwest as a hardy winter apple.

look.description: Medium to large, somewhat ribbed yellow apple, striped and mottled with orange-red.

taste.summary: White, fairly firm but coarse and very juicy flesh with a mildly acid, faintly aromatic flavour; rated only fair to good in quality.

pollination.notes: The National Fruit Collection records full bloom around 9 May, so group 3 is inferred.

climate.best_climates: Cold continental climates of the upper Midwest, where its Duchess parentage gives winter hardiness.
climate.poor_climates: Hot summers and mild winters; inferred from its northern origin.

grow_notes: A hardy, late-keeping heirloom for cold gardens. Pick in early October and store for winter use.

name: Pine Golden Pippin
history: A British dessert apple first recorded in 1861; its exact origin is not known. It is held in the National Fruit Collection.

look.description: Small, flattish golden apple with a good deal of russet.

taste.summary: Moderately firm, juicy yellowish flesh with a fairly sweet, rich and aromatic flavour and a light tart sparkle; one description notes a honey scent.

tree.notes: Average vigour, upright-spreading, spur-bearing and a good cropper (Orange Pippin).

pollination.notes: Late flowering: Orange Pippin lists group 5 and the National Fruit Collection records full bloom around 18 May. Needs a late-flowering partner.

climate.best_climates: Cool temperate and mild, damp climates with moderate summers; late flowering helps it avoid spring frost.
climate.poor_climates: Hot summers are likely to blunt its aroma (inferred); mild-winter regions lack chill.

health.other: Rated average for disease resistance by Orange Pippin; no specific weakness recorded.

grow_notes: A late-blooming russeted dessert apple suited to frosty gardens. Pair with another group 4-6 diploid.

name: Pott's Seedling
history: Raised by Samuel Potts at Ashton-under-Lyne around 1849. It has been suggested as the unconfirmed parent of James Grieve. The National Fruit Collection also lists Holland Pippin and Dean's Codlin among its synonyms.

look.description: Large, plain pale green to yellow apple with a glossy skin that bruises easily.

taste.summary: Soft, fine, greenish-white flesh with a clear acidity. Cooks down to a smooth puree that needs little sugar, while holding enough acid to keep slices from browning.

tree.notes: Grower reports mention crops that vary from year to year and a tree that stayed healthy without spraying.

pollination.notes: The National Fruit Collection records full bloom around 12 May, so group 3 is inferred.

climate.best_climates: Cool, moist northern English climates like the one it was raised in.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented; probably unsuited to hot or mild-winter regions.

health.other: No formal disease ratings found. The fruit bruises easily.

grow_notes: An early cooking apple from north-west England. Handle the fruit gently and use it within a few weeks.

name: Primus

origin.parentage: Reinette Rouge Etoilee x Cox's Orange Pippin

history: Raised in 1935 at Wageningen in the Netherlands from the Dutch Sterappel (Reinette Rouge Etoilee) and Cox's Orange Pippin.

look.description: Large, conical yellow apple striped orange-red, with russet dots and streaks and a slightly greasy skin.

taste.summary: Soft, coarse, creamy-white flesh with a very sweet flavour.

pollination.notes: The National Fruit Collection records full bloom around 12 May, so group 3 is inferred.

climate.best_climates: Cool maritime north-west European climates like the Netherlands (inferred).

grow_notes: A rarely grown Dutch Cox seedling; treat it like a Cox-type dessert apple with a mid-season partner.

name: Quinte
history: Released in 1964 by the Smithfield Experimental Farm in Ontario as an early summer apple. It found a niche in cold climates such as Sweden but is too light-cropping for commercial use.

look.description: Medium, slightly tall yellow apple mostly washed with light red.

taste.summary: Tender, creamy-white flesh, sweet but with a clear tart edge; one Swedish account compares the texture to sorbet. A good early apple that should be eaten straight from the tree.

tree.notes: Low yields keep it out of commercial orchards (Swedish Wikipedia).

pollination.notes: Early flowering: Orange Pippin lists group 2 and the National Fruit Collection records full bloom around 6 May. Swedish sources name Discovery, Katja, Summerred and White Transparent as pollinators.

climate.best_climates: Cold-temperate climates such as Ontario and southern to central Sweden (Swedish zones I-IV).
climate.poor_climates: Areas with heavy cedar-apple rust pressure; hot summers would hurry and soften an already short-lived early apple.

health.other: Susceptible to cedar-apple rust (Orange Pippin) and powdery mildew (Swedish Wikipedia).

grow_notes: An early-August apple for cold gardens. Plant with another early-flowering variety and eat the fruit within a couple of weeks.

name: Redwell

origin.place: University of Minnesota Fruit Breeding Farm, Excelsior, Minnesota
origin.parentage: Uncertain: the National Fruit Collection records Scott's Winter x unknown; Orange Pippin gives a Wealthy x Alexander seedling.

history: Raised around 1911 at the University of Minnesota fruit breeding farm and released in 1946. Sources disagree about its parentage.

look.description: Large, slightly elongated apple, streaked red to orange-red over yellow-green.

taste.summary: Soft, greenish to cream flesh with a mild, gently acid flavour; described as smooth and mellow, good for eating and baking.

pollination.notes: Fairly late flowering: the National Fruit Collection records full bloom around 15 May, so group 4 is inferred.

climate.best_climates: Cold continental climates like Minnesota, for which it was bred.
climate.poor_climates: Hot summers and mild winters (inferred from its origin).

grow_notes: A hardy, mild-flavoured Minnesota apple that keeps until about January. Plant with a later-flowering partner.

name: Regent

origin.place: University of Minnesota Fruit Breeding Farm, Excelsior, Minnesota
origin.parentage: Daniels Red Duchess x Delicious (National Fruit Collection); Orange Pippin gives Haralson x McIntosh

history: Released by the University of Minnesota in 1963-64 as a hardy, long-keeping apple for eating and cooking. Its published parentage differs between sources.

look.description: Medium to large, conical apple striped bright red over yellow-green.

taste.summary: Crisp, crackling and juicy cream flesh, sweet and honeyed but with plenty of acidity for balance. Holds its shape when cooked, with a light, sweet, fruity flavour.

tree.notes: Moderately vigorous and easy to train (University of Minnesota); precocious, spur-bearing heavy cropper (Orange Pippin).

pollination.notes: Orange Pippin lists group 3; the National Fruit Collection records full bloom around 11 May.

climate.best_climates: Cool-summer continental climates such as Minnesota and the northern US; rated moderately hardy there.
climate.poor_climates: Hot summers (inferred); the very coldest Minnesota sites, where it is only moderately hardy.

health.other: Susceptible to apple scab; some fire blight susceptibility; very resistant to cedar-apple rust (Orange Pippin).

grow_notes: A good keeper for cold gardens that crops early and heavily. Spray or site it for scab control, and thin heavy crops.
